source_text: Qui ita concedunt, recogitare debent de statu uocabuli ipsius. quid est mulier a primis quidem litteris sanctorum commentariorum? iam inueniunt sexus esse nomen, non gradum sexus; siquidem Euam nondum uirum expertam deus mulierem et feminam cognominauit, feminam, qua sexus generaliter, mulierem, qua gradus sexus specialiter. ita quoniam tunc innupta adhuc Eua mulieris uocabulo fuit, commune id uocabulum et uirgini factum est. nec mirum, si apostolus eodem utique spiritu actus, quo cum omnis scriptura diuina, tum et illa Genesis digesta est, . eadem uoce usus est mulierem ponendo, quae exemplo Euae innuptae et uirgini competat. cetera denique consonant. nam et hoc ipso, quod uirgines non nominauit, sicut alio in loco, ubi de nubendo docet, satis praedicat de omni muliere et de toto sexu dictum, nec distinctum esse inter mulierem et uirginem, quam omnino non nominat. qui enim alibi distinguere meminit, ubi scilicet differentia postulat (distinguit autem utramque speciem suis uocabulis designans), ubi non distinguit, dum utramque non nominat, nullam uult differentiam intellegi. quid? quod Graeco sermone, quo litteras apostolus fecit, usui est mulieres uocare quam feminas, id est γυναῖκας quam θηλεiας. igitur si pro sexus nomine uocabulum istud frequentatur, quod est in interpretatione pro eo quod est femina, sexum nominauit, dicens γυναῖκα. in sexu autem et uirgo contingitur. sed et manifesta pronuntiatio est: omnis, inquit, mulier adorans et prophetans intecto capite dedecorat caput suum. quid est omnis mulier, nisi omnis aetatis, omnis ordinis, omnis condicionis? nihil mulieris excipit dicendo omnis, sicut nec uiri nec uelandi; perinde enim omnis uir inquit. sicut ergo in masculino sexu sub uiri nomine etiam inuestis uelari uetatur, ita et in feminino sub nomine mulieris etiam uirgo uelari iubetur. aequaliter in utroque sexu minor aetas maioris sequatur disciplinam, aut uelentur et uirgines masculi, si non uelantur et uirgines feminae, quia nec isti nominatim tenentur; aliud sit uir et inuestis, si aliud est mulier et uirgo. nempe propter angelos ait uelari oportere, quod angeli propter filias hominum desciuerunt a deo. quis ergo contendat solas mulieres, id est nuptas iam et uirginitate defunctas, concupiscentiae esse, nisi si non licet et uirgines specie praestare et amatores inuenire? immo uideamus, ne uirgines solas concupierint, cum dicat scriptura filias hominum, quia potuit uxores hominum nominasse uel feminas indifferenter. etiam quod ait: et acceperunt sibi in uxores, eo facit, quod accipiuntur in uxores quae uacant scilicet. de non uacantibus autem aliter enuntiasset. itaque uacant tam uiduitate quam et uirginitate. adeo sexum nominando generaliter filias, et species in genere commiscuit. item cum dicit naturam ipsam docere uelandum feminis esse, quae capillum pro tegumento et ornamento mulieribus assignarit, nonne idem tegumentum et idem honor capitis uirginibus quoque adscriptus est? si mulieri turpe est radi, et uirgini perinde. in quibus ergo una condicio capitis deputatur, una et disciplina capitis exigitur, etiam ad eas uirgines, quas pueritia defendit; a primo enim femina nominata est. sic denique et Israel obseruat. sed si non obseruaret, nostra lex ampliata atque suppleta defenderet sibi adiectionem. uirginibus quoque iniciens uelamentum excusetur. nunc aetas, quae sexum suum ignorat, simplicitatis priuilegium teneat. nam et Eua et Adam, ubi eis contigit sapere, texerunt statim quod agnouerant. certe in quibus iam pueritia mutauit, sicut naturae, ita et disciplinae debet aetas esse munifica. nam et membris et officiis mulieribus resignantur. nulla uirgo est ex quo potest nubere, quoniam aetas iam in ea nupsit suo uiro, id est tempori. sed aliqua se deo uouit. tamen et crinem exinde transfigurat et omnem habitum ad mulieris conuertit. totum ergo asseueret et totum uirginis praestet: quod propter deum abscondit, plene obumbret. interest nostra, quod dei gratia exerceatur, solius dei conscientiae commendare, ne, quod a deo speramus, ab homine compensemus. quid denudas ante deum quod ante homines tegis? uerecundior eris in publico quam in ecclesia? si dei gratia est, et accepisti, quid gloriaris, inquit, quasi non acceperis? quid alias ostentatione tui iudicas? an alias gloria tua ad bonum inuitas? atqui et ipsa periclitaris amittere, si gloriaris, et alias ad eadem pericula cogis. facile eluditur quod affectione gloriae assumitur. uelare uirgo, si uirgo es; debes enim erubescere. si uirgo es, plures oculos pati noli. nemo miretur in tuam faciem; nemo mendacium tuum sentiat. bene mentiris nuptam, si caput ueles. immo mentiri non uideris; nupsisti enim Christo. illi carnem tuam tradidisti, age pro mariti tui disciplina. si nuptas alienas uelari iubet, suas utique multo magis. sed non puta institutionem uniuscuiusque antecessoris commouendam. multi alienae consuetudini prudentiam suam et constantiam eius addicunt. ne compellantur uelari, certe uoluntarias prohiberi non oportet; quae se etiam uirgines negare non possunt, concedo abuti in fama sua conscientiae apud deum securitate. de illis tamen, quae sponsis dicantur, constanter super meum modulum pronuntiare contestarique possum uelandas ex ea die esse qua ad primum uiri corpus osculo et dextera expauerint. omnia enim in his praenupserunt, et aetas per maturitatem, et caro per aetatem, et spiritus per conscientiam, et pudor per osculi experimentum, et spes per expectationem, et mens per uoluntatem. satisque nobis exemplo Rebecca est, quae sponso demonstrato tantum notitiae eius nubendo uelata est.
orientation: Tertullian is answering those who say the apostle required only married women to be veiled, by arguing from the word 'woman' itself.
pass_a_gloss: Those who grant this must reconsider the status of the word itself. What is 'woman' from the very first letters of the holy commentaries? Already they find that it is a name of the sex, not a degree of the sex; since indeed God called Eve, not yet having known a man, 'woman' and 'female': 'female,' by which the sex generally, 'woman,' by which a degree of the sex specifically. So since then Eve, still unmarried, was under the name of 'woman,' that name has also become common to the virgin. Nor is it surprising, if the apostle, moved by the same spirit by which both all divine Scripture and that Genesis was composed, used the same word in putting 'woman,' which by the example of unmarried Eve suits also the virgin. The rest finally agree. For by this very fact, that he did not name virgins, as in another place, where he teaches about marrying, he sufficiently declares that it was said about every woman and about the whole sex, and that no distinction was made between woman and virgin, whom he does not name at all. For he who elsewhere remembers to distinguish, where namely the difference demands (he distinguishes by designating each kind with its own words), where he does not distinguish, while he does not name either, he wants no difference to be understood. What? Because in the Greek language, in which the apostle wrote the letters, it is customary to call them 'women' rather than 'females,' that is gynaikas rather than theleias. Therefore if that word is used for the name of the sex, which is in translation for that which is 'female,' he named the sex, saying gynaika. But in the sex the virgin also is included. But also the pronouncement is clear: 'Every woman,' he says, 'praying and prophesying with uncovered head disgraces her head.' What is 'every woman' except of every age, of every rank, of every condition? He excepts nothing of woman by saying 'every,' just as neither of man nor of veiling; for likewise he says 'every man.' Therefore just as in the male sex under the name of 'man' even the unbearded is forbidden to be veiled, so also in the female under the name of 'woman' even the virgin is ordered to be veiled. Equally in both sexes let the lesser age follow the teaching of the greater, or let male virgins also be veiled, if female virgins are not veiled, because neither are these held by name; let 'man' and 'unbearded' be one thing, if 'woman' and 'virgin' is another. Surely he says that one must be veiled because of the angels, because the angels fell away from God on account of the daughters of men. Who then would contend that only women, that is those already married and dead to virginity, are objects of desire, unless it is not permitted for virgins also to excel in beauty and to find lovers? Rather let us see whether they desired virgins alone, since Scripture says 'daughters of men,' because it could have named 'wives of men' or 'females' indifferently. Also what it says: 'and they took for themselves as wives,' makes for this, that those who are taken as wives are those who are free. But about those not free it would have spoken otherwise. Therefore they are free both by widowhood and by virginity. So by naming the sex generally 'daughters,' he also mixed the kinds in the genus. Likewise when he says that nature itself teaches that females must be veiled, which assigned hair as a covering and ornament to women, has not the same covering and the same honor of the head been assigned to virgins also? If it is shameful for a woman to be shaved, so for a virgin likewise. Therefore in those for whom one condition of the head is reckoned, one teaching of the head is required, even for those virgins whom childhood defends; for from the beginning she was named 'female.' So finally Israel also observes it. But if it did not observe it, our law, enlarged and supplemented, would defend for itself the addition, imposing the veil on virgins also; let it be excused. Now let the age which does not know its own sex hold the privilege of simplicity. For both Eve and Adam, when it happened to them to know, covered immediately what they had recognized. Certainly in those in whom childhood has already changed, as of nature, so also of teaching the age ought to be mindful. For they are signed over to women by members and by duties. No one is a virgin from the time she can marry, since her age has already married in her to its own husband, that is to time. But someone has vowed herself to God. Nevertheless she also transforms her hair from then on and turns her whole dress to that of a woman. Therefore let her assert the whole and perform the whole of a virgin: what she hides for God's sake, let her fully overshadow. It is in our interest, that the grace of God be exercised, to commend it to the conscience of God alone, lest what we hope from God we repay from man. Why do you uncover before God what you cover before men? Will you be more modest in public than in church? If it is the grace of God, and you have received it, why do you glory, he says, as if you had not received it? Why do you judge others by your display? Or does your glory invite others to the good? But you yourself are in danger of losing it, if you glory, and you force others into the same dangers. What is assumed by desire of glory is easily mocked. Veil yourself, virgin, if you are a virgin; for you ought to blush. If you are a virgin, do not wish to endure many eyes. Let no one wonder at your face; let no one perceive your lie. You lie well that you are married, if you veil your head. Rather you will not seem to lie; for you have married Christ. To him you have handed over your flesh; act according to the teaching of your husband. If he orders other men's brides to be veiled, his own much more. But do not think that the institution of each predecessor must be disturbed. Many surrender their own prudence and its constancy to another's custom. Lest they be compelled to be veiled, certainly the willing ought not to be forbidden; those who cannot deny that they are virgins, I grant to abuse their reputation with security of conscience before God. About those, however, who are said to be betrothed, I can firmly pronounce and testify beyond my small measure that they must be veiled from that day on which they have shuddered at the first body of a man with a kiss and right hand. For in these all things have married beforehand: age through maturity, flesh through age, spirit through conscience, modesty through the experience of a kiss, hope through expectation, mind through will. And Rebecca is enough as an example for us, who, when her betrothed was shown, was veiled for the knowledge of him by marrying.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'woman' for mulier, and the whole argument turns on this word as a name of the sex.
Tertullian distinguishes femina as the general sex term from mulier as a degree; 'female' preserves that distinction.
The glossary requires 'teaching' for disciplina, and here it means the rule of Christian practice.
Inuestis means one not yet bearded, a youth; 'unbearded' keeps the literal physical sense Tertullian uses for the male parallel.
Vacare here means to be unmarried or unattached; 'are free' captures the sense of availability for marriage.
Expavescere means to be struck with awe or fear; 'have shuddered at' keeps the strong physical reaction Tertullian describes at first contact.

pass_b_english: Those who grant this exemption should think carefully about the meaning of the word itself. What is a woman, from the very first pages of the sacred writings? They will find that it is a name of the sex, not a degree of the sex. For God called Eve a woman and a female before she had known a man: female as the general name of the sex, woman as a particular name of the sex. So since Eve was still unmarried when she received the name woman, that word became common to the virgin as well. No wonder, then, that the apostle, moved by the same Spirit who composed all divine Scripture and that passage in Genesis, used the same word when he said woman, a word that fits the virgin too through the example of unmarried Eve.

Everything else agrees with this. By not naming virgins, as he does elsewhere when he teaches about marrying, he makes clear enough that he is speaking of every woman and the whole sex, and that no distinction is made between a woman and a virgin, whom he does not name at all. For when he remembers to distinguish elsewhere, where the difference requires it—and he distinguishes both kinds by naming each with its own word—when he does not distinguish and does not name either one, he wants no difference to be understood.

What about this? In the Greek language in which the apostle wrote, it is customary to say women rather than females—that is, gynaikas rather than theleias. So if this word is regularly used as the name of the sex, standing in for female, then he named the sex when he said gynaika. And the virgin is included in the sex.

The statement is also perfectly clear. Every woman, Paul says, who prays or prophesies with uncovered head dishonors her head (1 Corinthians 11:5). What is every woman but every age, every rank, every condition? By saying every he excludes no woman, just as he excludes no man and no veiling; for he likewise says every man (1 Corinthians 11:4). So just as in the male sex the unbearded youth is forbidden to veil under the name man, in the female sex the virgin is commanded to veil under the name woman. Let the younger age follow the teaching of the older equally in both sexes. Or let male virgins be veiled too, if female virgins are not veiled, since they too are not named explicitly. A man and an unbearded youth would be different things, if a woman and a virgin are different things.

He says, of course, that veiling is necessary because of the angels, since the angels fell away from God because of the daughters of men (Genesis 6:1–4). Who would argue that only women—that is, those already married and dead to virginity—are objects of desire? Unless virgins are not allowed to excel in beauty and find lovers? Let us rather consider whether they desired virgins alone, since Scripture says daughters of men, when it could have said wives of men or females without distinction. And when it says they took them as wives (Genesis 6:2), it points to this: those who are taken as wives are those who are free to marry. It would have spoken differently about those who were not free. So they are free both through widowhood and through virginity. Thus by naming the sex generally as daughters, he mixed the kinds within the genus.

Likewise when he says that nature itself teaches that females should be veiled, since it has assigned hair as a covering to women (1 Corinthians 11:14–15), has not the same covering and the same honor of the head been assigned to virgins too? If it is shameful for a woman to be shaved, it is equally so for a virgin (1 Corinthians 11:6). For those in whom one condition of the head is appointed, one teaching for the head is required—even for those virgins whom childhood protects. For from the beginning she was named female.

This is what Israel also observes. But if it did not observe it, our law, enlarged and completed, would claim the addition for itself. Let it be excused for placing the veil on virgins too. For now, let the age that does not know its own sex keep the privilege of simplicity. For Eve and Adam, when it happened that they knew, immediately covered what they had recognized (Genesis 3:7). Certainly in those whose childhood has changed, age ought to be generous to teaching just as it is to nature. For they are marked out for the members and duties of women. No one is a virgin from the time she can marry, since her age has already married her to its own husband—that is, to time.

But someone has vowed herself to God. Even so, from that point she changes her hair and turns her whole appearance to that of a woman. Let her then assert the whole thing and present herself entirely as a virgin: what she hides for God's sake, let her fully veil. It matters to us that God's grace be exercised, that we entrust it to the knowledge of God alone, so that we do not receive from men what we hope for from God. Why do you uncover before God what you cover before men? Will you be more modest in public than in the church? If it is God's grace and you have received it, why do you boast, as Paul says, as if you had not received it (1 Corinthians 4:7)? Why do you judge others by displaying yourself? Or does your glory invite others to what is good? But you yourself risk losing it if you boast, and you drive others into the same dangers. What is taken up out of love of glory is easily mocked.

Veil yourself, virgin, if you are a virgin; for you ought to blush. If you are a virgin, do not endure many eyes. Let no one wonder at your face; let no one perceive your lie. You lie well as a married woman if you veil your head. No—you do not seem to lie; for you have married Christ. To him you have handed over your flesh; act according to your husband's teaching. If he commands other men's brides to be veiled, how much more his own.

But do not think the institution of any predecessor should be disturbed. Many surrender their own wisdom and constancy to another's custom. Even if they cannot be compelled to veil, those who are willing should certainly not be forbidden. Those who cannot deny they are virgins—I allow them the misuse of their reputation, with their conscience secure before God. But about those who are said to be betrothed, I can declare and testify beyond my own measure: they must be veiled from the day they first shuddered at the body of a man with a kiss and a handshake. For in them everything has been married beforehand: age through maturity, flesh through years, spirit through consciousness, modesty through the experience of a kiss, hope through expectation, mind through will. And Rebecca is example enough for us: when her betrothed was pointed out, she was veiled for marriage at the mere knowledge of him (Genesis 24:65).

fixed: Source: 'feminam, qua sexus generaliter, mulierem, qua gradus sexus specialiter.' The English 'woman as a particular degree of the sex' misstates the source: 'gradus sexus' means a degree or stage of the sex, not a name. The argument is that 'woman' is a name of the sex, not a degree of the sex. Fixed to 'woman as a particular name of the sex' to match the source's contrast between general and particular names.

Source: 'quod accipiuntur in uxores quae uacant scilicet.' The English 'those who are free' is ambiguous. The source 'uacant' means 'are free' in the sense of unoccupied or available for marriage. Fixed to 'free to marry' to clarify.

Source: 'quoniam aetas iam in ea nupsit suo uiro, id est tempori.' The English 'married her to her husband—that is, to time itself' is close but the source says 'suo uiro' (its own husband). Fixed to 'its own husband' to match the source.

Source: 'de illis tamen, quae sponsis dicantur.' The English 'called betrothed' is accurate; 'sponsis' means betrothed. No change needed to the meaning, but adjusted to 'said to be betrothed' to match the source's 'dicantur' more closely.

Source: 'quae capillum pro tegumento et ornamento mulieribus assignarit.' The source does say 'tegumento et ornamento' (covering and ornament), so the English was correct. However, the confirmed problem about 1 Cor 11:15 saying only 'covering' is a scripture citation issue, not a mistranslation of Tertullian's text. Tertullian adds 'ornamento' himself. The English correctly renders Tertullian's words. No edit made to the scripture citation, but the phrase 'covering and ornament' is Tertullian's own wording, not a quotation of 1 Cor 11:15. The English is accurate to the source.

notes.quote: Every woman, he says, who prays or prophesies with uncovered head
notes.why: 'He' is Paul but not identified at first encounter in this section.

notes.quote: No one is a virgin from the time she can marry, since her age has already married her to her husband—that is, to time.
notes.why: 'Married her to her husband—that is, to time' is confusing; 'husband' = 'time' is unclear.
notes.fix: Render: 'her age has already betrothed her—to the passage of time itself.'

notes.quote: I grant them the abuse of their reputation
notes.why: 'Abuse of their reputation' is odd; likely means 'the misuse' or 'the burden' of their reputation.
notes.fix: Render: 'I allow them the misuse of their reputation' or 'the strain on their reputation'.

notes.quote: the angels fell away from God because of the daughters of men (1 Corinthians 11:10)
notes.why: 1 Cor. 11:10 mentions angels but does not say they fell; the fall is from Genesis 6:1–4.
notes.fix: Cite Genesis 6:1–4 for the fall; 1 Cor. 11:10 only for 'because of the angels'.

notes.why: Reader may not know 'betrothed' is a technical category of virgins formally promised in marriage.
notes.fix: Gloss: 'those who are called betrothed (virgins formally engaged to be married)'.

notes.quote: Let the younger age follow the teaching of the older equally in both sexes—or let male virgins be veiled too, if female virgins are not veiled, since they are not held by name either.
notes.why: Long conditional argument is hard to follow; 'held by name' is unclear.
notes.fix: Render: 'since they too are not named explicitly' and break into shorter sentences.

notes.quote: what she hides for God's sake, let her fully overshadow
